title: Understanding Python Modules and Reuse
learningObjectives: Explain module concepts and reusable code and where it is useful in Python programs.
Choose correct Python syntax for module concepts and reusable code.
Predict the result of representative PY16.1 operations.
Identify namespace, import and maintenance risks related to module concepts and reusable code.

understand.concept: A Python module is a file or importable module object that groups related names such as functions, classes and constants. Importing a module lets another part of a program reuse that code through a clear namespace instead of copying definitions. Python also provides built-in and standard-library modules.
understand.whyItMatters: Modules divide a program into maintainable units, make code easier to test and reduce duplication. A clear module boundary also helps teams understand which code owns each responsibility.
understand.analogy: A module is like a labelled toolbox: related tools are stored together and another program can request the tools it needs.
understand.analogyLimit: A real Python module also has import rules, namespaces, execution behaviour and caching that a physical toolbox does not represent.
understand.summary: Understanding Python Modules and Reuse teaches how Python organizes and reuses related code.

explain.narrative:
## What a module represents
A module is an importable namespace. A `.py` file can define functions, classes and variables; importing it makes those names available through the module object.

## Module categories
Built-in modules are available as part of the interpreter, while the standard library supplies modules such as `math`, `statistics`, `pathlib` and `json`. A project can also define its own modules. Third-party modules are installed separately and should be selected from trusted sources.

## Import behaviour
Python locates a module using its import system and search path. The first import normally executes the module's top-level statements and creates a module object; later imports in the same interpreter generally reuse the cached object in `sys.modules`.

## Good design
Keep module responsibilities focused, avoid surprising work at import time, and expose a small, understandable interface. Do not name a project file after a standard-library module such as `json.py` or `random.py`.

examples.title: Inspect a standard-library module
examples.explanation: The module object exposes a name and reusable constants.

examples.title: Use two modules for separate jobs
examples.code:
import math
import statistics
values = [2, 4, 6]
print(math.sqrt(81))
print(statistics.mean(values))
examples.explanation: Different modules group different areas of functionality.

examples.title: Check that a module is an object
examples.explanation: An imported module is a module object with named attributes.

examples.title: Read a module's documentation string safely
examples.expectedOutput: This module provides access to the mathematical functions
examples.explanation: The module documentation describes its purpose; exact text can vary by Python version, so this should be reviewed against the pinned interpreter.

examples.title: Observe import caching
examples.code:
import math
import sys
print(sys.modules['math'] is math)
examples.explanation: The import system stores loaded modules in sys.modules.
